caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Malawi's debt went from relief to crisis in under two decades. HIPC completion in 2006 brought it to 17.9% of GDP, the series low. Then came Cashgate-era borrowing, kwacha devaluations that inflated the local-currency value of external debt, and repeated climate and COVID shocks: the ratio climbed relentlessly to 87.6% in 2024, the series high, easing to a projected 77.8% in 2025. Malawi is now in debt distress, with domestic debt (expensive Treasury bills) the acute pressure point. Restructuring discussions have dragged on, and debt service crowds out everything else in the budget.
inflation_management: Malawi's inflation history is one of repeated devaluation-driven spirals. It was contained at 7-9% from 2007 to 2011, then the 2012 kwacha devaluation (under Joyce Banda) sent it to 21.3% in 2012 and 28.3% in 2013. Tighter policy brought it back to single digits by 2018-2021, but forex shortages, Cyclone Freddy, and drought reignited it: 20.8% in 2022, 28.8% in 2023, and a series high of 32.2% in 2024, with 28.4% projected for 2025. The Reserve Bank of Malawi has hiked rates aggressively, but with chronic forex scarcity and a managed exchange rate under constant pressure, monetary policy fights pass-through it cannot prevent.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt to 17.9% of GDP.
President Bingu wa Mutharika died in office; Joyce Banda devalued the kwacha; inflation surged past 20%.
'Cashgate' corruption scandal saw donors withdraw budget support.
2019 election annulled by the courts; Lazarus Chakwera won the 2020 rerun.
Cyclone Freddy (2023) and drought devastated agriculture; inflation hit 28.8%.
September 16, 2025: Peter Mutharika (85) defeated Chakwera with 56.8% of the vote, returning to power on the economic crisis.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued distress management: debt near 78% of GDP, inflation near 30%, and growth hostage to rains and forex. Upside depends on a credible debt restructuring and the new Mutharika government's stabilization plan; downside is a disorderly currency collapse. Uncertainty is high: Malawi has the policies of a crisis country but not yet the resolution of one, and the 2025 political reset is untested.
